q: NOM-070 recognises three production classes of Mezcal. Name them, and state what forces a bottle into the strictest one.
accept: mezcal artesanal and ancestral with ancestral requiring clay pot distillation
three classes and ancestral demands pit roasting and clay pot stills
mezcal mezcal artesanal mezcal ancestral clay still and direct fire for ancestral
ancestral artesanal and plain mezcal ancestral keeps the fibres and uses clay pots
ans: Mezcal, Mezcal Artesanal and Mezcal Ancestral. Ancestral is the strictest: agave cooked in an earthen pit, milled by mallet or tahona, fermented in stone, wood, clay or hide with the fibres present, and distilled in clay pots over direct fire — no copper column anywhere in the process
exp: The plain 'Mezcal' class is the permissive one: autoclaves, diffusers and column stills are all legal there, which is how industrial mezcal reaches supermarket price points without lying on the label. Artesanal sits between — pit or masonry oven, copper or clay pot still. Reading the class on the back label tells you more about the liquid in front of you than the agave species does.

opts: Jalisco entire, plus municipalities in four other states
Jalisco and Oaxaca entire, plus parts of Guerrero
Jalisco entire only, with no municipalities elsewhere
Jalisco entire, plus municipalities in nine other states
exp: All of Jalisco, plus listed municipalities in Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas — four other states. The sprawling map belongs to Mezcal, not Tequila: Mezcal's DO began with five states in 1994 and has been extended repeatedly since, to nine at the usual count and further after that. Borrowing Mezcal's reach for Tequila is the misconception under test. Two more numbers to hold alongside it: Tequila must be at least 51% Blue Weber agave, so '100% de agave' marks a real legal distinction from mixto rather than a marketing flourish, and everything must be distilled within the DO.

q: Japanese whisky's labelling standards took effect in 2021. What do they require, and what is their legal status?
accept: mashed fermented distilled and matured in japan for three years bottled at forty percent
three years in wood under 700 litres all done in japan and the rules are voluntary
made and aged in japan minimum three years but these are industry rules not legislation
distilled and matured in japan bottled at 40 percent and it is a voluntary standard
ans: Water drawn in Japan; malted grain always in the mash; saccharification, fermentation and distillation carried out in Japan at under 95% abv; maturation in Japan for at least three years in wooden casks of no more than 700 litres; bottling in Japan at 40% abv or more. Their status is the sting: they are voluntary industry-association standards, not law, binding only member companies, with the transition period closing in 2024
exp: The standards exist because Japanese tax law defined whisky loosely enough that shochu, bulk imported Scotch and neutral spirit could legally be bottled and sold as 'Japanese whisky'. Because compliance is voluntary, a non-member can still ignore them entirely — so on the floor, check whether the producer belongs to the association and whether the bottle names an actual distillery. Know the rules and know they have no teeth.

q: Irish Single Pot Still whiskey's mash bill must contain:
opts: At least 51% malted barley, the balance unmalted
At least 30% malted and 30% unmalted barley
Only malted barley, distilled three times
At least 30% unmalted barley, with no malt minimum
exp: The unmalted barley is the whole point of the style: it began as a dodge around a nineteenth-century tax on malt and stayed because it delivers that oily, creamy texture and green-apple bite. The technical file also caps other cereals at 5%, a limit fought over for years by producers wanting more latitude. Redbreast and the Spot bottlings are the references. Triple distillation is a house habit in Ireland, not a legal requirement — Cooley proves it.
